mentions.quote: the king, free from envy, should be impartial to all beings, observing the vow of Yama
mentions.role: exemplar of impartiality invoked as a model for the king

entities.description: The deity Yama, whose vow of impartiality the king is enjoined to emulate when adjudicating legal disputes.
entities.justification: Yama is explicitly named as a divine exemplar whose conduct (his vow) the king must observe in the conduct of justice.

mentions.quote: Māṇḍavya, though not a thief, acquired the character of one through legal procedure
mentions.role: historical cautionary example of wrongful conviction by legal process

entities.description: A sage cited as a canonical case of an innocent man wrongly branded a thief through defective legal procedure.
entities.justification: Māṇḍavya is named as a real named figure whose miscarriage of justice illustrates the danger of flawed legal proceedings.

mentions.quote: the interest on these is unlimited, so said Manu Prajāpati
mentions.role: cited authority for the rule on unlimited interest on certain commodities

entities.description: Manu Prajāpati, the primordial lawgiver, cited as the authority for the rule that interest on bricks and certain goods is unlimited.
entities.justification: Manu Prajāpati is explicitly named as the source of a specific legal ruling on interest rates.

mentions.quote: This is the introduction to legal procedure, first declared by the Self-existent One
mentions.role: divine originator of the Nāradasmṛti's legal introduction

entities.description: The Self-existent One (Svayambhū/Brahmā), credited as the primordial declarer of the framework of legal procedure set out in the Mātṛkā.
entities.justification: The text explicitly attributes the foundational legal introduction to the Self-existent One, marking the text's divine authority.

mentions.quote: The specific wealth of a Brāhmaṇa is known to be of three kinds: what is received by accepting gifts, from sacrificial fees, and from pupils
mentions.role: social group with prescribed lawful means of wealth acquisition

mentions.quote: A Brāhmaṇa should never perform the work of a Śūdra, nor a Śūdra the work of a Brāhmaṇa
mentions.role: caste whose occupational restrictions are defined

mentions.quote: A Brāhmaṇa who sells what is forbidden for sale has fallen from the path
mentions.role: subject of commercial prohibitions

mentions.quote: Those of Śūdra origin who bring false accusations against twice-born men
mentions.role: victims of false accusations by Śūdras

entities.description: The priestly varna, whose lawful occupations, commercial prohibitions, debt obligations, and ritual prerogatives are extensively regulated throughout this window.
entities.justification: Brāhmaṇas appear repeatedly as the primary subjects of caste-specific rules governing wealth, commerce, occupation, and social standing.

mentions.quote: They declare the specific wealth of a Kṣatriya also to be of three kinds: what is obtained in battle, taxes, and fines from legal proceedings
mentions.role: social group with prescribed lawful means of wealth acquisition

entities.description: The warrior-ruler varna whose lawful wealth sources are battle-spoils, taxes, and judicial fines.
entities.justification: Kṣatriyas are named as a distinct group with their own tripartite wealth categories distinct from those of the other varnas.

mentions.quote: The specific wealth of a Vaiśya is also known to be of three kinds: from agriculture, cattle-rearing, and commerce
mentions.role: social group with prescribed lawful means of wealth acquisition

mentions.quote: A Vaiśya may overcome a calamity by the practice of usury if he wishes
mentions.role: group permitted usury in times of calamity

entities.description: The merchant-farmer varna whose lawful wealth derives from agriculture, cattle, and commerce, and who alone (among twice-born) may practice usury in extremity.
entities.justification: Vaiśyas are repeatedly distinguished as a group with specific occupational privileges and permissions around usury that differ from Brāhmaṇas.

mentions.quote: For a Śūdra, it is through service to these
mentions.role: lowest varna whose lawful wealth is service to higher varnas

mentions.quote: Those of Śūdra origin who bring false accusations against twice-born men, the king should have their tongues cut out
mentions.role: group subject to severe punishment for false accusation against twice-born

entities.description: The servile varna whose only lawful wealth-source is service, and who faces extreme bodily punishment for false accusations against twice-born men.
entities.justification: Śūdras are named explicitly in two contrasting rules — their restricted occupational sphere and their disproportionate punishment — marking their inferior legal status.

mentions.quote: the king was made the wielder of the rod of punishment and the overseer of disputes
mentions.role: institutional origin of royal judicial authority

mentions.quote: the king, free from envy, should be impartial to all beings, observing the vow of Yama
mentions.role: ideal judge required to embody Yama's impartiality

mentions.quote: All subjects are dependent; the lord of the earth is independent
mentions.role: apex of legal independence

entities.description: The king is the ultimate judicial authority, wielder of the rod of punishment, apex of independent persons, and subject of extensive norms governing impartial adjudication.
entities.justification: The king recurs throughout as the institutional locus of judicial power and the primary subject of obligations regarding impartial justice.

mentions.quote: It was given to him by me while he was on the Gandhamādana mountain
mentions.role: example of an unverifiable, impractical location cited to illustrate a defective plaint

entities.description: The mythological mountain Gandhamādana, cited as an example of an unrealistic location that renders a legal plaint unprovable and therefore invalid.
entities.justification: Gandhamādana is explicitly named as a place so remote or legendary that a claim grounded in it falls outside 'practical Dharma' and cannot be established.

mentions.quote: Putting the Dharmaśāstra first, and abiding by the opinion of the chief judge
mentions.role: primary normative source the king must consult

mentions.quote: Where there is a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra, one should discard the rule of the Arthaśāstra
mentions.role: superior source in the hierarchy of legal authority

entities.description: The genre of sacred jurisprudential texts (law books) that constitutes the primary normative source for legal procedure, superior to the Arthaśāstra.
entities.justification: Dharmaśāstra is repeatedly invoked as the authoritative text-genre the king must follow and that overrides the Arthaśāstra in case of conflict.

mentions.quote: Where there is a conflict between the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra, one should discard the rule of the Arthaśāstra
mentions.role: secondary normative source subordinate to Dharmaśāstra

mentions.quote: following a path that does not conflict with the Dharmaśāstra and the Arthaśāstra
mentions.role: co-authoritative practical guide for legal procedure

entities.description: The genre of political-economic treatises on governance and statecraft, treated as a secondary normative source for legal procedure subordinate to Dharmaśāstra.
entities.justification: The Arthaśāstra is named twice as a recognized but subordinate legal source, yielding to Dharmaśāstra when the two conflict.

themes.topic: Origins and decay of Dharma as the foundation of legal procedure

mentions.quote: When men were devoted solely to Dharma and were speakers of truth, then there was no legal procedure, nor hatred, nor envy
When Dharma was lost among men, legal procedure was introduced

themes.justification: The text opens by grounding the very existence of legal procedure in the historical decline of Dharma, framing the whole juridical system as a response to moral degeneration.

themes.topic: Hierarchy of legal authority: Dharma, procedure, custom, royal edict

mentions.quote: Dharma, legal procedure, custom, and royal edict—this legal procedure has four feet; each succeeding one overrules the preceding one
Therein, Dharma is based on truth; legal procedure on witnesses; custom on what is recorded by the people; and the royal edict on the king's command

themes.justification: The fourfold hierarchy of sources is the structural spine of the entire jurisprudential framework presented in Mātṛkā 1.

themes.topic: The king's duty of impartial and dharmic adjudication

mentions.quote: the king, free from envy, should be impartial to all beings, observing the vow of Yama
For a king of purified soul who settles legal disputes according to Dharma, seven virtues arise, like the seven flames of a fire

themes.justification: The text repeatedly enjoins the king to conduct judicial proceedings impartially and in accordance with Dharma, listing the spiritual and worldly rewards for doing so.

themes.topic: Procedural fairness: plaint, counter-plaint, evidence, and decision

mentions.quote: The essence of legal procedures is said to be the formal claim. If it fails, the plaintiff is defeated; by proving it, he becomes the victor
Evidence is said to be of two kinds: human and divine. Human evidence consists of documents and witnesses; divine evidence is remembered as the ordeal by balance and so on

themes.justification: A systematic account of how a legal dispute is initiated, how the parties must state their cases, what forms of evidence are admissible, and how a verdict is rendered runs through Mātṛkā 1 and 2.

mentions.quote: A Brāhmaṇa should never perform the work of a Śūdra, nor a Śūdra the work of a Brāhmaṇa. For both of them, these are acts that cause loss of caste
The specific wealth of a Vaiśya is also known to be of three kinds: from agriculture, cattle-rearing, and commerce. For a Śūdra, it is through service to these

themes.justification: The section on wealth classification ties legal liability and legitimate economic activity explicitly to varna identity, making caste hierarchy a structural feature of the property law exposition.

themes.topic: Debt inheritance and familial liability across generations

mentions.quote: A debt incurred by an undivided paternal uncle or brother, or by the mother for the sake of the family, all the heirs must pay
A debt of the grandfather, which has come down in due succession and has not been paid by the sons, the grandsons shall pay; it ceases with the fourth descendant

themes.justification: A substantial portion of the first chapter of the Eighteen Topics is dedicated to tracing the transmission of debt obligations through family lines, defining how far generational responsibility extends.

themes.topic: The three categories of wealth and their moral valence

mentions.quote: It is known to be of three kinds: white, speckled, and black
That which is acquired through bribery, gambling, dacoity, fraud, forgery, crimes of violence, or by any deceitful means, is declared to be black

themes.justification: The tripartite classification of wealth into white (virtuous), speckled (mixed), and black (sinful) introduces a moral-cosmological dimension into the law of property and debt.

themes.topic: Documentary evidence: validity, defects, and probative weight

mentions.quote: A written document, witnesses, and possession are remembered as the three kinds of evidence, by which a creditor recovers his wealth
A document made by one who is intoxicated, accused of a crime, a woman, a child, or by force, is not a valid instrument

themes.justification: The text devotes an entire concluding sequence to the rules governing documentary evidence — when documents are valid, what defects invalidate them, and how they rank against other proofs.

themes.topic: Legal competence, dependency, and the status of minors, women, and slaves

mentions.quote: One who has not reached the age of legal competence is not liable for debt, even if he is independent
Likewise, an act done by a slave is considered not done, unless by the master's command, for a slave is not his own master

themes.justification: The text systematically defines who is legally competent to incur debt or make valid transactions, drawing sharp distinctions between independent agents and those — women, sons, slaves, minors — whose acts require a superior's authority.

themes.topic: Possession, title, and the ten-year limitation on property claims

mentions.quote: Whatever property a creditor sees being enjoyed by others for ten years, while he remains silent, he is not entitled to recover it
Where possession is seen without title, and no title is seen anywhere, title is the cause there, not possession

themes.justification: The extended discussion of possession (bhoktṛtva) as a form of evidence introduces a doctrine of adverse possession qualified by the requirement of title, structuring the relationship between factual control and legal right.

themes.topic: Sin and spiritual consequences of judicial misconduct

mentions.quote: A quarter of the adharma goes to the perpetrator, a quarter goes to the witness, a quarter goes to all the court assessors, and a quarter goes to the king
a court assessor, having entered the assembly, free from passion and hatred, should speak such words that he does not fall into hell

themes.justification: The text embeds legal procedure within a karmic framework, making the spiritual pollution of adharma transferable among all actors in a corrupt proceeding — a theological underpinning of judicial ethics that is implicit rather than the surface topic.

themes.topic: Usury, interest-rate categories, and commodity-specific lending rules

mentions.quote: The giving and taking of a loan is desired for the sake of the profit from its location. This is called usury, and by it is the livelihood of usurers
It is remembered in the sacred texts as being of four kinds: physical interest, periodical interest, stipulated interest, and compound interest

themes.justification: The Nāradasmṛti includes a detailed taxonomy of interest types and commodity-specific rate ceilings, framing commercial lending within a dharmic regulatory scheme.

citations.quote: the interest on these is unlimited, so said Manu Prajāpati
citations.justification: Manu Prajāpati is named as the authority for the rule that interest on bricks and certain listed goods is unlimited, constituting an explicit appeal to the Manusmṛti tradition.
